item.description: It may be true that the smallest production cars ever built make modern compacts look huge, but everything's relative. The tiniest new car you can get for 2026 in the U.S. — the Fiat 500e — is still quite small when compared to most other rides today.

It may be true that the smallest production cars ever built make modern compacts look huge, but everything's relative. The tiniest new car you can get for 2026 in the U.S. — the Fiat 500e — is still quite small when compared to most other rides today. Oh, and speaking of tiny, that word applies to the current Fiat lineup as well. It only includes the 500e and the adorable Fiat Topolino low-speed vehicle that was designed for stunting on your suburban neighbors – not traveling on U.S. highways.

The all-electric city car is a mere 142.95 inches long and 74.12 inches wide (including its mirrors), and its height is 66.3 inches. Note that the 2026 Mini Cooper is even more vertically challenged, as it checks in at 57.6 inches in height, yet it's nearly 16 inches longer and roughly 3.5 inches wider than the 500e. Meanwhile, for comparison's sake, one of the biggest new passenger vehicles available right now is another EV, the Cadillac Escalade IQL — a 750-horsepower, 19-foot-long American luxury beast . To be exact, the IQL stretches a tick over 19 feet, at 228.5 inches, and it's a whopping 94.1 inches wide.

The sub-compact crossover is getting a $2,000 price increase to go along with its facelift for the 2027 model year , and I'm here to tell you that it actually makes sense. You can relax. It's OK.

The Trax might cost 8.5% more than it did a year ago, now starting at $25,495 (including destination) for the base LT trim, but a big chunk of that increase comes from the fact that the previous base model, the LS, has been dropped, according to Car and Driver . Chevy has trimmed the Trax's vast lineup from five trim levels to three. In any case, along with the new entry-spec LT, the Activ and RS trims (now condensed into one trim versus the old 1RS and 2RS) will soldier on, both starting at $28,295.

Unless you've been living under the proverbial rock for the last decade, you're sure to have seen the myriad inexpensive electric dirt bikes ripping around city streets and countryside alike. With inexpensive lithium batteries and compact, lightweight electric motors providing wheel-standing torque with a twist of the wrist, these things tend to be both quick and incredibly fun to ride. When it comes to fun-per-dollar, it's difficult to argue that these don't peg the needle squarely in the as-much-as-you-want zone. However, to keep costs low, manufacturers tend to skip most of the equipment and paperwork you would need for them to be legally plated and ridden on the street.

Most of these electric dirt bikes come fresh off the boat from China. You've heard of the big names, like Surron or Talaria, I'm sure. Even American electric motorcycle brand Zero's XE and XB off-road motorcycles are built in China. These days there are dozens of other manufacturers building (or white-label reselling) these machines for distribution through just about every online retailer you can think of.

Briefing: Equipping a sports car with a big and powerful engine is all well and good. But if the car in question is designed like a cinder block, then it's just wasting the engine's potential. As a car speeds up, the air resistance around it increases.

Equipping a sports car with a big and powerful engine is all well and good. But if the car in question is designed like a cinder block, then it's just wasting the engine's potential. As a car speeds up, the air resistance around it increases. And a car with a sleeker design can slip through the air with less resistance, thus granting it better performance. That, in a very basic nutshell, is why aerodynamics matter.

Now, drag coefficient (Cd) isn't the be-all and end-all when it comes to measuring a car's aerodynamics as a whole. Something like drag area, which combines that metric with frontal area measurements, provides a more complete picture. Nevertheless, drag coefficient scores still provide a solid impression as to just how slippery a car is — and such figures are more readily available from automakers, too.

Imagining a collage of objects of American culture, the mind conjures up images of things like sports stadiums, a drive-thru menu, the Wall Street Bull, the Hollywood sign, blue jeans, apple pie, and likely, some kind of car. Cars, our car dependency, and the American love for V8 engines are integral to our culture, and there are no cars to demonstrate this better than the pony car family. While very similar, there are some differences between a muscle car and a pony car.

To put it simply, the muscle car and the pony car are two sides of the same coin. The muscle car was bigger and purely focused on looking cool and going fast, with not much thought to anything else. The pony car took all that was fun about the muscle car, including the good looks and exciting performance, and made it all a bit easier to live with, often by being smaller than its muscle car counterparts. The Mustang started the pony car trend, but it wasn't the only one to do it. Since those early days in the 1960s, we've seen different takes from different manufacturers, including models like the Chevrolet Camaro, the Dodge Challenger, and even some from the hands of Carroll Shelby. Many of these models have stuck around to the modern day. The spirit of the pony car is old, but it is far from gone.

The Tesla Cybertruck is one of the most polarizing vehicles of our time, largely due to its unconventional silhouette and the lack of curves on its stainless steel body. Besides grabbing the attention of onlookers, owners have another thing to worry about that has to do with maintenance costs — the tires. Changing the rubber on your Tesla pickup truck requires a higher budget than your average full-size truck, and can exceed the $2,000 mark on flagship trims. Furthermore, the Cybertruck's tires might need to be replaced sooner than expected due to its immense weight and torque figures.

Of course this is not limited to Tesla, as the Rivian R1T suffers from similar issues. According to Tesla's manual, the entry-level Cybertruck with 18-inch wheels wears all-season Goodyear Wrangler Territory HT rubber (285/70R18). Stepping up to 20-inch wheels, you can either have all-season Pirelli Scorpion ATR tires (285/65R20), or the heavier-duty Goodyear Wrangler Territory R/T (LT285/65R20). The latter feature a bespoke sidewall design tailored for the wheel covers of the Cybertruck . Finally, owners in cold regions can opt for the 20-inch Goodyear Wrangler DuraTrac R/T.

If you're in France, you really need to look out for the drunk deer.

Deer are a hazard drivers have to contend with. Sure, we could put some murder kitties in the forests, because more big cats in forests can reduce car crashes by roughly 75% . Or, we could install crossings to give creatures a safe path over big roads, like they did in California with the world's largest wildlife crossing . But short of that, accidents with deer will happen. State Farm reports that there were more than 1.6 million animal-related collisions between July 2025 and July 2026. It is a real concern.

Pontiac had helped launch the muscle-car era in 1963 — when it debuted the GTO package for its 1964 Pontiac Tempest LeMans coupe — and the brand followed that up with the Firebird pony car in 1967. item.title: Here's Why Fuel Economy Drops So Much At 75 MPH
item.dc:creator: Elena Rostova
item.description: It is a well known fact that combustion vehicles have greater fuel economy ratings on the highway rather than in urban driving scenarios. However, this reality can be easily reversed if you exceed a certain speed threshold. ELF targeted property and managed to avoid causing serious physical harm to anyone in hundreds of credited attacks from the late 1990s through the 2000s. The government branded ELF a terrorist group, partly because ELF used destructive tactics like arson, which is a common tool of militant groups . And, in fact, multiple SUVs were set on fire that night in 2003.

Either way, the government knew they were looking for passionate environmentalists. Within just a couple of weeks, the feds arrested a suspect, Josh Connole. So when these ports produce a comprehensive assessment of future marine fuels and leave hydrogen out of their detailed deep-sea shipping plans, it deserves attention well beyond California.

The Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , released in October, is the product of a substantial examination of shipping fleets, carrier preferences, fuel availability and infrastructure costs. The ports recommend developing commercial methanol bunkering demonstrations, continuing existing ship-to-ship LNG bunkering arrangements and avoiding major new fuel terminals until demand becomes credible. Hydrogen, the molecule that California has spent so much money promoting for transportation, did not make the cut for detailed quantitative deep-sea fuel planning.

Every year, the little road closes to vehicle traffic due to the influx of scaly travelers. Not once, but twice every trip around the sun. In fact, it's the only known road in the United States to shut down in observance of a reptile migration. The shutdown isn't meant to protect the national forest's human visitors, either – it's to make sure the road-going snakes can complete their journey unharmed.

If you're into cars, and particularly driving and wrenching on older cars , you'll have doubtless come across old wives' tales about driving and running them. Examples include older vehicles being safer, even though they lack modern safety equipment like airbags, because they're made of thicker steel. Or that filling up with high octane fuel will boost the horsepower of even the most ordinary engine. Both are generally untrue, but what about the one that says leaving a car battery on concrete can damage it?

Like those other two examples, the battery myth is just that. You won't hurt a battery by leaving it on a concrete floor. But also like the safety and octane stories, there's a grain of truth to it. Modern cars are designed to crumple to absorb impacts, and that can make them look less safe after a relatively small accident. And some performance cars, or tuned cars, do deliver more output with higher octane fuel. Which is why, by the same token, even today, you might hear the concrete floor battery warnings repeated by folks who have more experience in looking after cars than you do.

The rules surrounding speed limit signs are standard across the country, but how they're followed can vary. The rules, however, are fairly clear. The federal government doesn't set speed limits, even on interstates. Instead, states and local municipalities depend on traffic engineers to help decide posted speed limits. Those are determined by considering laws, the areas where the speed limit will be posted, and the safety of the area, including the flow of traffic and frequency of accidents. (Not, though, the long-touted "85th-percentile rule." )

Traffic engineers often refer to their bible, the 1,100-page-plus Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices , written and revised by the Federal Highway Administration. If you're curious, turn to Page 84 of the revised 11th edition, where the section "Speed Limit Signs and Plaques" resides. The item to pay attention to is number 14: "Speed Limit (R2-1) signs, indicating speed limits for which posting is required by law, shall be located at points of change from one speed limit to another."

If you look at the lineage of Aston Martin's main production grand tourer over the years, it goes straight from the DB9 of the 2000s and early 2010s to the DB11 in 2016. A few years before the DB11 came along, work was underway on Daniel Craig's fourth James Bond movie, "Spectre." Director Sam Mendes, who helmed the wildly successful and, by most accounts, very good "Skyfall," was returning, and he wanted a new Aston Martin for Bond to drive. Enter the DB10, a car that was originally a concept sketch for the next Vantage , but became its own special model brought to life specifically for the movie. Fun fact: this was apparently the very first time an entirely new car was made for a Bond film.

Getting pulled over is never a fun time. The reasons are seemingly endless, from driving a police magnet to dangling a keepsake from the rearview mirror or having Flock misidentify your car as stolen . Now imagine going through any of these scenarios while also having a disability that creates communication challenges, such as autism. For someone with sensory, cognitive, and verbal difficulties, the already stressful event of being pulled over could lead to trauma or even being shot. And for the police officer, being unaware of the driver's medical condition can lead to miscommunication and mishandling of the situation.

That's why the Blue Envelope Program was developed: to improve communication between law enforcement and people who require additional accommodations or time during stops. Designed to be an all-inclusive information tool that's easy and straightforward to use for both the driver and officer, on the envelope's exterior are printed instructions and guidelines regarding how to interact with one another, while inside are essential documents, such as a driver's license, proof of insurance, and vehicle registration.

If you're an avid golfer but find the time spent between holes a bit uncomfortable, Tractor Supply has something that will make your life a lot nicer. Available right now for $15,849 is the Massimo MVR Cargo Max HVAC Lithium, an enclosed electric vehicle that, as its name suggests, includes integrated heating and air conditioning. Tractor Supply has it listed under its "Golf Carts" section of vehicles, but per its product description, its intended use is a lot wider.

The MVR is said to be "built for farm chores, property maintenance and recreation," and meant to let its owner "tackle property projects in comfort." And in that context, it really does remind me of a kei truck , especially with its power-dump cargo bed that uses a hydraulic mechanism for easier unloading.

Briefing: It's probably been two decades since you've used a floppy disk — unless you're managing air traffic or preparing to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. The Federal Aviation Administration, a bit behind the technology curve, announced Thursday that it will finally phase out 3.5-inch floppy disks at air traffic control facilities.

It's probably been two decades since you've used a floppy disk — unless you're managing air traffic or preparing to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. The Federal Aviation Administration, a bit behind the technology curve, announced Thursday that it will finally phase out 3.5-inch floppy disks at air traffic control facilities. The agency aims to rid itself of the antiquated technology by the end of 2028. In its place, air traffic controllers will have a modern, fully digitized system at their disposal.

The FAA plans to replace four legacy systems that date back to the 1980s with the Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) at 435 locations. The transition has already happened at Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and a pair of data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. These older systems were simply no longer sustainable to operate. Air traffic control currently depends, in part, on Compaq computers running on Windows 95.
